items.stem: In an impedance (Coulter principle) counter, how is each blood cell detected and sized as it passes through the aperture?
options: It scatters laser light; scatter intensity is proportional to cell volume
It lowers electrical resistance; pulse height is proportional to hemoglobin
It raises electrical resistance; pulse height is proportional to cell volume
It absorbs light at 540 nm; absorbance is proportional to the cell number
items.why: Cells are poor electrical conductors suspended in a conductive diluent. Each cell passing through the aperture briefly **increases resistance between the electrodes**, producing a voltage pulse. The number of pulses gives the count, and pulse height is proportional to cell volume.

whyNot.0: Laser light scatter is the optical method, not the impedance (Coulter) principle.
whyNot.1: Cells are poor conductors, so they raise resistance; pulse height reflects volume, not hemoglobin content.
whyNot.3: Absorbance at 540 nm is used to measure hemoglobin after lysis, not to count or size cells.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., automated blood cell analysis chapter (electronic impedance)

items.stem: A woman with severe iron deficiency (MCV 64 fL before treatment) received 2 units of red cells yesterday. Today the analyzer reports an MCV of 70 fL and a high RDW, and the RBC histogram shows two separate peaks. What best explains the histogram?
options: Platelet clumps and giant platelets being counted as small red cells
Two populations: her microcytic cells plus transfused normocytic cells
Red cell agglutination caused by a cold-reacting autoantibody
A uniform shift of all of her red cells toward a larger size
items.why: A bimodal (dimorphic) RBC histogram means two populations of different cell volume. After transfusion, **the donor's normocytic cells and the patient's microcytic cells** form separate peaks. The MCV is the average of both, so it can look less abnormal, while the RDW is high.

whyNot.0: These distort the low-volume end of the RBC histogram near its threshold; they would not form a second population of normal red cell size.
whyNot.2: Agglutinates are counted as single very large cells, giving a falsely high MCV and MCHC and a low RBC count, not two populations.
whyNot.3: A uniform shift would move a single peak to the right; it would not split the curve into two separate peaks.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., automated blood cell analysis chapter (histograms and RDW)

items.stem: An adult has pancytopenia, an MCV of 118 fL, and a low reticulocyte count. The smear shows oval macrocytes, Howell-Jolly bodies, and several neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Oval macrocytes plus **hypersegmented neutrophils** indicate megaloblastic anemia, in which impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation in all cell lines. Ineffective hematopoiesis explains the pancytopenia and low reticulocyte count. The most common causes are vitamin B12 and folate deficiency.

whyNot.0: Liver disease produces round (not oval) macrocytes and target cells and does not cause hypersegmented neutrophils.
whyNot.1: Reticulocytosis would give a high reticulocyte count and polychromasia, not pancytopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils.
whyNot.3: Iron deficiency causes a microcytic, hypochromic anemia, not a macrocytic one.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., megaloblastic and nonmegaloblastic macrocytic anemias chapter

items.stem: A patient with a severe infection has a WBC of 55 x 10^9/L with neutrophilia and a left shift to metamyelocytes and myelocytes. Which result most strongly favors a leukemoid reaction over chronic myeloid leukemia?
options: An increased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score
A decreased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score
An absolute basophilia on the differential
Detection of the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene
items.why: In a leukemoid reaction, normal activated neutrophils contain plenty of alkaline phosphatase, so the **LAP score is high**. CML neutrophils have little LAP activity, and CML also tends to show basophilia and the BCR-ABL1 fusion. Molecular testing for BCR-ABL1 is now the definitive way to tell them apart.

whyNot.1: A low LAP score is typical of chronic myeloid leukemia, so it would favor CML, not a leukemoid reaction.
whyNot.2: Basophilia (often with eosinophilia) is a characteristic feature of CML, not of a reactive leukocytosis.
whyNot.3: BCR-ABL1 is the defining genetic lesion of CML and would confirm CML.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., nonmalignant leukocyte disorders and myeloproliferative neoplasms chapters

items.stem: On day 7 of unfractionated heparin after hip surgery, a patient's platelet count falls from 260 to 100 x 10^9/L and a new leg vein thrombosis appears. What is the mechanism of the most likely disorder?
options: Autoantibodies to glycoprotein IIb/IIIa that cause splenic platelet clearance
IgG antibodies to platelet factor 4-heparin complexes that activate platelets
Heparin-induced suppression of megakaryocyte production in the marrow
Dilution of platelets by intravenous fluids and transfused blood products
items.why: A platelet drop of more than 50% starting 5 to 10 days after heparin exposure, with new thrombosis, is typical of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. **IgG antibodies bind PF4-heparin complexes** and activate platelets through Fc receptors, causing low platelets and thrombosis at the same time. Heparin must be stopped and a non-heparin anticoagulant started.

whyNot.0: This describes immune thrombocytopenia, which is not linked to heparin timing and causes bleeding rather than thrombosis.
whyNot.2: Heparin does not suppress megakaryopoiesis, and decreased production would not explain new thrombosis.
whyNot.3: Dilution occurs right after surgery and transfusion, not on day 7, and it does not cause thrombosis.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (thrombophilia) chapters

items.stem: Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin activates protein C. With protein S as a cofactor, activated protein C limits clotting by inactivating which factors?
options: Factor VIIa bound to tissue factor
items.why: Activated protein C, with protein S, cleaves and inactivates the cofactors **Va and VIIIa**, slowing the tenase and prothrombinase complexes. Factor V Leiden resists this cleavage, which is why it increases the risk of thrombosis.

whyNot.0: Thrombin and Xa are inhibited mainly by antithrombin, whose action is accelerated by heparin.
whyNot.1: The tissue factor-VIIa complex is inhibited by tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI).
whyNot.3: These are not substrates of activated protein C; fibrin is broken down by plasmin.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., normal hemostasis and coagulation chapter (control of coagulation)

items.stem: Which protein, released by endothelial cells, converts fibrin-bound plasminogen to plasmin to start fibrinolysis?
items.why: **tPA** binds fibrin together with plasminogen, so it activates plasminogen mainly where a clot is present. The plasmin formed digests fibrin into degradation products, including D-dimer from cross-linked fibrin.

whyNot.0: PAI-1 does the opposite: it inhibits tPA and slows fibrinolysis.
whyNot.1: Alpha-2-antiplasmin inhibits free plasmin; it does not form plasmin.
whyNot.2: TAFI slows fibrinolysis by removing lysine residues on fibrin that bind plasminogen and tPA.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., normal hemostasis and coagulation chapter (fibrinolysis)

items.stem: A specimen drawn through a central venous line gives an APTT above 150 s. The thrombin time is markedly prolonged, but the reptilase time is normal. What best explains these results?
items.why: The thrombin time is very sensitive to heparin because heparin-antithrombin inhibits the added thrombin. Reptilase (batroxobin) also converts fibrinogen to fibrin but **is not inhibited by heparin**. A long thrombin time with a normal reptilase time therefore points to heparin, here probably from the line, and the specimen should be recollected by venipuncture.

whyNot.1: A low fibrinogen level, whatever its cause, would prolong both the thrombin time and the reptilase time.
whyNot.2: An abnormal fibrinogen molecule usually prolongs both the thrombin time and the reptilase time.
whyNot.3: Factor VIII deficiency prolongs the APTT but leaves the thrombin time normal, because added thrombin bypasses factor VIII.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., laboratory evaluation of hemostasis chapter (thrombin time, reptilase time)

items.stem: A woman with two prior venous thromboses and no bleeding history has a prolonged APTT that does not correct immediately on a 1:1 mix with normal plasma. A dilute Russell viper venom time (dRVVT) is prolonged and shortens markedly when excess phospholipid is added. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Lupus anticoagulants are antiphospholipid antibodies that prolong phospholipid-dependent clotting tests in vitro but are associated with thrombosis. Failure of the mix to correct shows an inhibitor, and **correction of the dRVVT by excess phospholipid** confirms that the inhibitor is phospholipid-dependent.

whyNot.0: A factor VIII inhibitor causes bleeding, is typically time- and temperature-dependent, and is not corrected by extra phospholipid.
whyNot.2: A factor deficiency corrects on mixing with normal plasma, and the dRVVT does not depend on factor XII.
whyNot.3: The APTT in von Willebrand disease corrects on mixing, and the disorder causes bleeding rather than thrombosis.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., laboratory evaluation of hemostasis and thrombophilia chapters; CLSI H60 (Laboratory Testing for the Lupus Anticoagulant)

items.stem: In the Clauss fibrinogen assay, diluted patient plasma is clotted with a high concentration of thrombin. How is the clotting time related to the result?
options: It is directly related to fibrinogen, since more fibrinogen clots more slowly
It mainly reflects prothrombin, since thrombin is generated in the cuvette
It is inversely related to fibrinogen and read from a calibration curve
It mainly reflects factor XIII, since detection requires a cross-linked clot
items.why: Plasma is diluted (usually 1:10) and excess thrombin is added so that **fibrinogen is the only rate-limiting factor**. The more fibrinogen present, the shorter the clotting time, and results are read from a curve made with calibrator plasma of known fibrinogen concentration.

whyNot.0: More fibrinogen gives a faster clot, so the relationship is inverse, not direct.
whyNot.1: Thrombin is added in excess, which bypasses the patient's own prothrombin.
whyNot.3: The endpoint is the first fibrin formation, which does not depend on factor XIII cross-linking.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., laboratory evaluation of hemostasis chapter (fibrinogen assay)

items.stem: A pregnant patient with impaired kidney function is receiving enoxaparin, a low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). Which test is recommended if her anticoagulation must be monitored?
options: Anti-factor Xa assay calibrated for LMWH
Prothrombin time reported as an INR
Thrombin time with standard thrombin reagent
items.why: Most LMWH chains are too short to bridge antithrombin to thrombin, so LMWH acts mainly through **inhibition of factor Xa** and has little effect on the APTT. When monitoring is needed (renal impairment, pregnancy, extremes of body weight), a chromogenic anti-Xa assay with LMWH calibrators is used.

whyNot.1: The APTT is relatively insensitive to LMWH and does not reliably reflect its effect.
whyNot.2: The PT/INR is used to monitor warfarin and is largely unaffected by LMWH.
whyNot.3: LMWH has little anti-thrombin (anti-IIa) activity, so the thrombin time changes little and does not track the dose.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., antithrombotic therapy and monitoring chapter

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl has heavy menstrual bleeding and frequent nosebleeds; her mother has a similar history. Platelet count and size are normal, the PT is normal, and the APTT is slightly prolonged. Ristocetin-induced aggregation is markedly reduced and corrects when normal plasma is added; responses to ADP, collagen, and epinephrine are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Mucocutaneous bleeding in an autosomal dominant pattern, a mildly prolonged APTT (from low factor VIII, which VWF protects), and abnormal ristocetin aggregation suggest von Willebrand disease. **Correction with normal plasma** shows that the defect is in plasma VWF, not in the platelet GPIb receptor, which separates it from Bernard-Soulier syndrome.

whyNot.0: Bernard-Soulier syndrome shows giant platelets and often thrombocytopenia, and its ristocetin defect is in platelet GPIb, so normal plasma does not correct it.
whyNot.1: Glanzmann thrombasthenia gives absent aggregation with ADP, collagen, and epinephrine but a normal ristocetin response.
whyNot.2: Hemophilia A is X-linked, causes mainly joint and deep tissue bleeding, and has a normal ristocetin response.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., hemorrhagic disorders (von Willebrand disease) and platelet function testing chapters

items.stem: A hospitalized patient's MCV was 92 fL yesterday and is 71 fL today. The patient was not transfused, and quality control for both runs was acceptable. What is the most likely cause of this delta check failure?
options: Iron deficiency that developed since yesterday
The specimen belongs to a different patient
Mild in vitro hemolysis of the specimen
items.why: MCV is very stable within a person because red cells survive about 120 days, so a large overnight change without transfusion is not physiologically plausible. A delta check failure like this most often signals **a mislabeled or misidentified specimen**, which must be investigated before results are released.

whyNot.0: Red cells live about 120 days, so iron deficiency lowers the MCV gradually over weeks, not overnight.
whyNot.2: Acceptable QC shows the analyzer was calibrated correctly, and drift would affect all specimens, not just one.
whyNot.3: Hemolysis lowers the red cell count and hematocrit but would not shrink the remaining cells enough to drop the MCV by 21 fL.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., quality assurance in hematology chapter (delta checks)

items.stem: A hematology analyzer's performance is monitored by calculating a weighted moving average of patients' MCV, MCH, and MCHC in consecutive batches of 20 samples, without commercial control material. Which quality control method is this?
items.why: **Bull's algorithm (XB)** relies on the fact that the red cell indices of a large patient population stay stable over time. A shift in the moving average of 20-sample batches beyond its limits (commonly about plus or minus 3% of target) signals a calibration or reagent problem.

whyNot.0: A delta check compares a patient's current result with that same patient's previous result, not population averages.
whyNot.2: Levey-Jennings charts plot results of commercial control material against its mean and SD limits.
whyNot.3: Westgard rules are applied to control material results to accept or reject a run.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., quality assurance in hematology chapter (moving averages)

items.stem: A technologist phones a critical platelet count of 8 x 10^9/L to the nurse caring for the patient. What must be done to complete the critical-result report?
options: Have the nurse read back the result, then record who received it and when
Repeat the result twice so the nurse can write it down accurately
Release the result in the LIS; the phone call needs no further record
Ask the nurse to inform the physician later and end the call without a record
items.why: Critical results must be reported promptly to a responsible caregiver, and **read-back** confirms that the patient identity and value were heard correctly. The technologist documents the name of the person notified, the date and time, and that read-back was done.

whyNot.1: Repeating the result does not confirm that the nurse heard it correctly; the receiver must read it back.
whyNot.2: Critical-result notification must be documented, including who was notified and the time.
whyNot.3: The call must still be documented, and delaying the information defeats the purpose of a critical-value call.

items.ref: CLSI GP47 (Management of Critical- and Significant-Risk Results); Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., quality assurance chapter

items.stem: A patient with polycythemia has a hematocrit of 65%. A coagulation tube will receive 4.5 mL of whole blood. Using the CLSI formula C = (1.85 x 10^-3)(100 - Hct)(V), where C is the volume of 3.2% sodium citrate in mL and V is the volume of whole blood in mL, how much citrate should the tube contain?
items.why: C = 0.00185 x (100 - 65) x 4.5 = 0.29 mL. A high hematocrit means less plasma in the same blood volume, so the usual 0.5 mL of citrate would leave too much citrate for the plasma present. **The citrate volume must be reduced when the hematocrit is above 55%** so the citrate concentration in the plasma stays at the intended level, avoiding falsely prolonged PT and APTT.

whyNot.0: 0.50 mL is the standard amount for a 4.5 mL draw at a normal hematocrit; using it here would over-anticoagulate the small plasma volume.
whyNot.1: This result comes from multiplying by the hematocrit (65) instead of by the plasma fraction (100 - 65).
whyNot.2: 0.21 mL is the volume of citrate to REMOVE from a standard 0.5 mL tube, not the volume that should remain in it.

items.ref: CLSI H21 (Collection, Transport, and Processing of Blood Specimens for Testing Plasma-Based Coagulation Assays); Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on laboratory evaluation of hemostasis (specimen collection)

worked.problem: A patient's hematocrit is 60%. A pediatric coagulation tube will receive 2.7 mL of whole blood. Using C = (1.85 x 10^-3)(100 - Hct)(V), how much 3.2% citrate is needed, and how much must be removed from a tube that contains 0.3 mL?
worked.result: Keep 0.20 mL of citrate (remove 0.10 mL) before collecting 2.7 mL of blood

items.stem: A newborn needs a capillary heel puncture for a CBC. Which area of the heel is the recommended puncture site?
options: The posterior curvature of the heel
The medial or lateral edge of the plantar surface
The center of the plantar surface of the heel
The arch of the foot just in front of the heel
items.why: In infants the calcaneus lies very close to the skin, so the puncture must avoid the bone. **CLSI recommends the medial or lateral edge of the plantar (bottom) surface of the heel**, where the distance to bone is greatest. Punctures over the bone risk osteomyelitis.

whyNot.0: The posterior curve of the heel lies directly over the calcaneus and should never be punctured.
whyNot.2: The central plantar area overlies the calcaneus, so a puncture there could reach bone.
whyNot.3: The arch contains nerves, tendons, and vessels and is not an approved capillary puncture site.

items.ref: CLSI GP42 (Collection of Capillary Blood Specimens); Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on blood specimen collection

items.stem: From an RBC count of 3.50 x 10^12/L and a reticulocyte percentage of 3.0%, calculate the number of reticulocytes per liter of blood (the absolute reticulocyte count).
items.why: The absolute reticulocyte count converts the percentage into the number of reticulocytes per liter: RBC count x (reticulocyte % / 100). Here 3.50 x 10^12/L x 0.030 = 0.105 x 10^12/L = 105 x 10^9/L. **Multiplying the RBC count by the reticulocyte fraction removes the distortion that anemia causes in the percentage.**

whyNot.0: This treats 3.0% as 0.003 instead of 0.030, a decimal-point error that makes the result ten times too low.
whyNot.1: This keeps the right digits but the wrong power of ten: the product is 0.105 x 10^12/L, which equals 105 x 10^9/L, not 0.105 x 10^9/L.
whyNot.3: This treats 3.0% as 0.30 instead of 0.030, a decimal-point error that makes the result ten times too high.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on manual, semiautomated, and point-of-care testing in hematology (reticulocyte count)

worked.problem: RBC count 2.80 x 10^12/L; reticulocyte count 4.5%. Find the absolute reticulocyte count.
steps: Convert the percentage to a fraction: 4.5% = 0.045

items.stem: A Miller disc in the microscope eyepiece has a large square (A) and a small square (B) used for manual reticulocyte counts. What is the area of square B relative to square A, and what is counted in square B?
options: One-fourth of square A; reticulocytes only
One-ninth of square A; red cells only
One-ninth of square A; reticulocytes only
One-fourth of square A; red cells only
items.why: Square B is one-ninth the area of square A. Reticulocytes are counted in the large square A, and **all red cells are counted only in the small square B**, which keeps the red cell tally manageable. The reticulocyte percentage is then calculated with a factor of 9 to adjust for the area difference.

whyNot.0: Square B is one-ninth, not one-fourth, of square A, and reticulocytes are counted in square A.
whyNot.2: The area ratio is right, but reticulocytes are counted in the large square A, not in square B.
whyNot.3: Red cells are counted in square B, but its area is one-ninth, not one-fourth, of square A.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on manual, semiautomated, and point-of-care testing in hematology (Miller disc)

items.stem: In the Kleihauer-Betke test for fetal-maternal hemorrhage, a maternal blood smear is exposed to an acid buffer and then counterstained. Fetal red cells stain pink-red, while adult red cells look like pale ghosts. What explains this difference?
options: Hb F resists elution at acid pH, so it stays inside fetal cells
Fetal cells are larger, so they absorb more of the counterstain
Hb A resists elution at acid pH, so it stays inside adult cells
Adult cells are lysed by the alkaline counterstain used in the test
items.why: The test relies on the different behavior of hemoglobins in acid. **Hb F resists acid elution and remains in fetal cells**, which then take up the pink counterstain, while Hb A is washed out of adult cells and leaves empty ghosts. The ratio of fetal to adult cells is used to estimate the volume of fetal bleed.

whyNot.1: Cell size does not cause the staining difference; retained hemoglobin does.
whyNot.2: This reverses the principle: Hb A is the hemoglobin that is eluted by acid.
whyNot.3: The test uses an acid buffer, not an alkaline one, and the adult cells are eluted rather than lysed.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on hemoglobinopathies and thalassemias / fetal hemoglobin testing; AABB Technical Manual (fetal-maternal hemorrhage)

items.stem: A patient has chronic hemolysis, dark morning urine, and a hepatic vein thrombosis. On flow cytometry, a large population of her granulocytes fails to bind fluorescent aerolysin (FLAER) and lacks CD24. What does this finding indicate?
options: Inherited deficiency of red cell pyruvate kinase
IgG autoantibody bound to the red cell surface
Inherited deficiency of the band 3 red cell membrane protein
Loss of GPI-anchored proteins from an acquired PIGA mutation
items.why: FLAER binds directly to the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, and CD24 is a GPI-anchored protein on granulocytes. **Absence of FLAER binding and GPI-linked antigens on a clone of cells is diagnostic of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).** The acquired PIGA mutation leaves cells without CD55 and CD59, so complement lyses the red cells, and thrombosis is a major complication.

whyNot.0: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an enzyme defect diagnosed by enzyme assay; it does not affect GPI-anchored proteins.
whyNot.1: IgG coating of red cells (warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia) is detected by the direct antiglobulin test and does not remove GPI anchors from granulocytes.
whyNot.2: Band 3 deficiency (hereditary spherocytosis) is shown by reduced eosin-5'-maleimide binding to red cells, not by loss of FLAER on granulocytes.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on intrinsic defects leading to increased erythrocyte destruction (PNH); ICCS/ICSH guidelines for PNH flow cytometry

items.stem: A patient with chronic myeloid leukemia is on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Which method is used to quantify BCR-ABL1 transcripts and monitor molecular response with the greatest sensitivity?
options: Conventional G-banded karyotyping of marrow metaphases
Interphase FISH with BCR and ABL1 probes
items.why: BCR-ABL1 is expressed as an mRNA transcript, which RT-qPCR converts to cDNA and amplifies while measuring the amount in real time. **RT-qPCR can detect about one leukemic cell among 10,000 to 100,000 normal cells**, so it is the standard method for tracking molecular response and residual disease in CML.

whyNot.0: Karyotyping examines only about 20 metaphases, so it detects disease only when a sizable fraction of cells is abnormal.
whyNot.2: CD34 marks immature progenitor cells and does not identify the BCR-ABL1 fusion at all.
whyNot.3: Interphase FISH scores more cells than karyotyping, but it typically detects only about 1 abnormal cell among a few hundred nuclei scored.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapters on molecular diagnostics in hematopathology and myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML)

items.stem: A bone marrow aspirate from a patient with anemia and a dimorphic red cell population is stained with Prussian blue. Many erythroid precursors show blue granules forming a ring around the nucleus. Where is this iron located?
options: In ferritin dispersed in the cytoplasm
items.why: These cells are ring sideroblasts. When heme synthesis is impaired, iron accumulates inside the mitochondria, which lie close to the nucleus in erythroid precursors. **The perinuclear ring of Prussian blue-positive granules reflects iron-loaded mitochondria**, which is the hallmark of sideroblastic anemia.

whyNot.0: Normal sideroblasts contain a few scattered ferritin granules in the cytoplasm, not a perinuclear ring.
whyNot.1: Iron in macrophages represents storage iron, while ring sideroblasts are erythroid precursors.
whyNot.2: Iron does not deposit in the nuclear membrane; the ring forms because mitochondria cluster around the nucleus.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on disorders of iron kinetics and heme metabolism (sideroblastic anemia)

items.stem: A laboratory calibrates its microhematocrit centrifuge by spinning the same specimens for increasing times and reading the hematocrit after each run. How is the optimal spin time selected?
options: The time that gives the highest hematocrit reading
The time at which the result matches the analyzer hematocrit
The shortest time after which the hematocrit stops decreasing
The time at which the buffy coat first becomes visible
items.why: With longer spinning, red cells pack more tightly and the hematocrit falls until packing is complete. **The optimal time is the shortest spin after which further spinning gives no further decrease in hematocrit**, meaning maximal packing has been reached. Centrifuges are recalibrated periodically as part of preventive maintenance.

whyNot.0: The highest reading occurs with the shortest spin, when packing is incomplete and more plasma is trapped among the cells.
whyNot.1: The analyzer calculates hematocrit differently, so matching it does not show that the cells are fully packed.
whyNot.3: The buffy coat appears early, before red cell packing is complete.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on manual, semiautomated, and point-of-care testing in hematology (microhematocrit); CLSI H07 (Procedure for Determining Packed Cell Volume by the Microhematocrit Method)

items.stem: A specimen with a WBC count of 80 x 10^9/L gives a falsely high hemoglobin by the cyanmethemoglobin method because the solution is turbid. How can this error be corrected?
options: Read the absorbance at 415 nm instead of 540 nm
Extend the reaction time to 30 minutes before reading
Centrifuge the reagent-sample mixture and read the supernatant
Dilute the mixture 1:2 with Drabkin reagent and multiply by 2
items.why: Very high leukocyte counts make the cyanmethemoglobin solution cloudy, and the turbidity adds to the absorbance at 540 nm. **Centrifuging the reagent-sample mixture removes the cells, so the clear supernatant can be read accurately.** Lipemia, another cause of turbidity, is corrected instead by using patient plasma in the reagent blank.

whyNot.0: Changing wavelength does not remove turbidity, and 540 nm is the specified wavelength for cyanmethemoglobin.
whyNot.1: Longer incubation helps the slow conversion of carboxyhemoglobin but does nothing for turbidity from intact cells.
whyNot.3: Diluting the mixture lowers the hemoglobin and the turbidity in the same proportion, so the error remains.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on manual, semiautomated, and point-of-care testing in hematology (hemoglobin determination)

items.stem: During bone marrow culture for conventional karyotyping, which agent is added to stop dividing cells in metaphase?
items.why: Chromosomes are most condensed and easiest to analyze during metaphase. **Colcemid disrupts the mitotic spindle and arrests dividing cells in metaphase.** The cells are then swollen in hypotonic solution, fixed, spread on slides, and banded.

whyNot.0: Phytohemagglutinin is a mitogen that stimulates T lymphocytes in blood cultures to divide; it does not arrest them.
whyNot.1: Hypotonic KCl swells the cells so that the chromosomes spread apart; it is used after metaphase arrest.
whyNot.2: Trypsin partially digests chromosomal proteins to produce G-banding after the slides are made.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on cytogenetics

items.stem: Which marker, a nuclear enzyme, is expressed by precursor B and T lymphoblasts but not by mature lymphocytes?
items.why: TdT adds nucleotides during immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement, an early step in lymphoid development. **Nuclear TdT is a marker of immature lymphoid cells**, so it supports a diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukemia or lymphoblastic lymphoma and is absent in mature lymphoid neoplasms such as CLL.

whyNot.0: CD20 is a surface marker of mature B cells and is often weak or absent on B lymphoblasts.
whyNot.1: CD45 is a surface antigen on nearly all leukocytes, mature and immature, so it is not specific for blasts.
whyNot.2: Myeloperoxidase is a cytoplasmic enzyme of the myeloid lineage, not a lymphoid nuclear marker.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapters on flow cytometric analysis in hematologic disorders and precursor lymphoid neoplasms

items.stem: Alkaline cellulose acetate electrophoresis (pH 8.4-8.6) shows Hb A and a second band at the Hb S position. The hemoglobin solubility test is negative. On citrate agar at pH 6.0-6.2, the second band moves with Hb A. Which variant is most likely?
items.why: On alkaline electrophoresis, Hb S, Hb D, and Hb G migrate together. Acid citrate agar separates them: Hb S moves to its own position, whereas **Hb D and Hb G migrate with Hb A on citrate agar**. The negative solubility test also rules out Hb S, leaving Hb D as the best answer.

whyNot.0: Hb S would give a positive solubility test and would separate from Hb A on citrate agar.
whyNot.1: Hb C migrates with Hb A2, E, and O on alkaline electrophoresis, not at the Hb S position.
whyNot.3: Hb E migrates with Hb C and A2 on alkaline electrophoresis, not with Hb S.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on hemoglobinopathies (laboratory diagnosis of hemoglobin variants)

items.stem: In adults, hematopoietic (red) marrow is found mainly in the flat bones of the axial skeleton. Which site is preferred for bone marrow aspiration and core biopsy in an adult?
items.why: With age, active marrow in the long-bone shafts is replaced by fat, and hematopoiesis is concentrated in the pelvis, vertebrae, ribs, skull, and sternum. **The posterior iliac crest is the preferred adult site** because it has ample red marrow, is far from vital structures, and allows both aspiration and core biopsy.

whyNot.0: The sternum can be aspirated but is not used for core biopsy because the thin bone lies over the heart and great vessels.
whyNot.2: The anterior tibia is used only in infants; in adults the tibial marrow is fatty.
whyNot.3: The femoral shaft contains yellow (fatty) marrow in adults.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapters on hematopoiesis and bone marrow examination

items.stem: Which cytokine is the main growth factor for the production and differentiation of eosinophils?
items.why: Hematopoietic growth factors act on specific lineages. **Interleukin-5, produced mainly by Th2 lymphocytes, drives eosinophil production**, which explains eosinophilia in allergic and parasitic conditions.

whyNot.1: G-CSF mainly stimulates neutrophil production and release.
whyNot.2: Thrombopoietin regulates megakaryocyte growth and platelet production.
whyNot.3: Interleukin-7 supports the development of lymphocyte precursors.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on hematopoiesis (cytokines and growth factors)

items.stem: A person who moves to a high altitude has a rise in red cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). How does this change affect hemoglobin?
options: Lowers oxygen affinity; the curve shifts to the right
Raises oxygen affinity; the curve shifts to the left
Lowers oxygen affinity; the curve shifts to the left
Raises oxygen affinity; the curve shifts to the right
items.why: 2,3-BPG, made in the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, binds between the beta chains of deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the deoxy form. **More 2,3-BPG lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and shifts the dissociation curve to the right**, so more oxygen is released to the tissues.

whyNot.1: Higher oxygen affinity with a left shift occurs when 2,3-BPG falls, as in stored blood.
whyNot.2: Lower oxygen affinity corresponds to a right shift, not a left shift.
whyNot.3: A right shift means lower, not higher, oxygen affinity.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on hemoglobin metabolism (oxygen dissociation curve)

items.stem: What is the globin chain composition of fetal hemoglobin (Hb F)?
options: Two alpha and two delta chains
Two zeta and two epsilon chains
Two alpha and two gamma chains
Two alpha and two beta chains
items.why: Each hemoglobin is a tetramer of two alpha-like and two beta-like chains. **Hb F is alpha2 gamma2**, the main hemoglobin of fetal life; after birth gamma chain production falls and beta chains take over.

whyNot.0: Alpha2 delta2 is Hb A2, a minor adult hemoglobin.
whyNot.1: Zeta2 epsilon2 is Hb Gower-1, an embryonic hemoglobin made in the yolk sac period.
whyNot.3: Alpha2 beta2 is Hb A, the main adult hemoglobin.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on hemoglobin metabolism

items.stem: Within minutes after an epinephrine injection, a patient's absolute neutrophil count nearly doubles, with no increase in bands or younger forms. What explains this rise?
options: Neutrophils are released from the bone marrow storage pool
Marginated neutrophils detach into the circulating pool
Neutrophil production in the marrow mitotic pool increases
Neutrophils return from the tissues into the bloodstream
items.why: About half of the neutrophils in blood vessels are loosely attached to the endothelium (marginating pool) and are not counted in a CBC. **Epinephrine, stress, and exercise detach these cells into the circulating pool within minutes**, raising the count without a left shift.

whyNot.0: Release from the marrow storage pool takes hours and usually adds bands to the blood.
whyNot.2: Increased production in the mitotic pool takes days, not minutes.
whyNot.3: Neutrophils that enter the tissues do not return to the circulation.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on leukocyte development, kinetics, and functions

items.stem: After a neutrophil engulfs bacteria, its respiratory burst produces hydrogen peroxide. Which granule enzyme combines hydrogen peroxide with chloride ions to form hypochlorous acid?
items.why: The respiratory burst begins when NADPH oxidase makes superoxide, which is converted to hydrogen peroxide. **Myeloperoxidase from the primary granules converts hydrogen peroxide and chloride into hypochlorous acid**, a powerful microbicidal oxidant.

whyNot.1: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide into hydrogen peroxide, the step before hypochlorous acid formation.
whyNot.2: Lysozyme kills bacteria by breaking down cell wall peptidoglycan, not by oxidation.
whyNot.3: NADPH oxidase starts the burst by producing superoxide; it does not form hypochlorous acid.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on leukocyte development, kinetics, and functions (neutrophil killing)

items.stem: In a healthy person, about what fraction of the body's platelets is held in the spleen at any time?
items.why: **About one-third of platelets are pooled in the spleen**, exchanging freely with the two-thirds in the circulation. With splenomegaly the pool can grow large enough to cause thrombocytopenia, and after splenectomy the platelet count rises.

whyNot.0: One-tenth underestimates the normal splenic platelet pool.
whyNot.1: One-half overestimates the normal splenic pool.
whyNot.3: Two-thirds is the fraction circulating in the blood, not the fraction held in the spleen.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on megakaryopoiesis and platelet production

items.stem: A single dose of aspirin impairs platelet function for the life of the platelet. Which enzyme does aspirin irreversibly acetylate, and which product is lost?
options: Thromboxane synthase, blocking thromboxane A2 formation
Phospholipase A2, blocking arachidonic acid release
items.why: Platelet activation releases arachidonic acid, which cyclooxygenase-1 converts to prostaglandin endoperoxides and then thromboxane A2. **Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1**, and because platelets lack a nucleus they cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts about 7 to 10 days.

whyNot.0: The P2Y12 ADP receptor is blocked by thienopyridines such as clopidogrel, not by aspirin, and it is a receptor rather than an enzyme.
whyNot.1: Thromboxane synthase acts after cyclooxygenase and is not the enzyme aspirin acetylates.
whyNot.2: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids and is not inhibited by aspirin.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on platelet structure and function

items.stem: On a Wright-stained smear, the red cells look blue-gray, the leukocyte nuclei are very dark, and the eosinophil granules appear gray-blue rather than orange-red. What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Wright stain combines acidic eosin with basic methylene blue, and the buffer pH sets the balance between them. **An overly alkaline buffer, a thick smear, or prolonged staining makes the whole smear too blue.** The fix is to check and correct the buffer pH and adjust the smear thickness and staining time.

whyNot.0: An acidic buffer gives the opposite pattern: bright red cells, pale nuclei, and brilliant orange eosinophil granules.
whyNot.1: Water in the methanol fixative produces refractile, moth-eaten artifacts in red cells, not overall blue staining.
whyNot.2: Too much rinsing removes stain and leaves the smear pale, not intensely blue.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on peripheral blood smear preparation and staining

items.stem: A burn patient's impedance platelet count is 410 x 10^9/L, but the smear estimate is about 150 x 10^9/L. The smear shows many schistocytes and microspherocytes, and the platelet histogram does not return to baseline at its upper threshold. What explains the discrepancy?
options: Red cell fragments in the platelet size range counted as platelets
Giant platelets being excluded from the count as red cells
Platelet clumps being counted as single large platelets or as leukocytes
EDTA-dependent antibodies forming platelet rings around neutrophils
items.why: Impedance analyzers classify particles by volume, and very small red cells or fragments overlap the platelet size range. **Schistocytes and microspherocytes counted as platelets falsely raise the impedance platelet count**, and the histogram tail that stays elevated at the upper threshold flags the interference. An optical or immunologic platelet count or a smear estimate should be used instead.

whyNot.1: Giant platelets counted as red cells also lower the platelet count, the opposite of what is seen here.
whyNot.2: Platelet clumps lower the platelet count because several platelets are counted as one particle or as a leukocyte.
whyNot.3: Platelet satellitism removes platelets from the counting channel and falsely lowers the count.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on automated blood cell analysis (sources of error)

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes Hb H disease?
options: Two alpha genes are deleted; excess gamma chains form tetramers
Four alpha genes are deleted; excess beta chains form tetramers
Three alpha genes are deleted; excess beta chains form tetramers
Three alpha genes are deleted; excess gamma chains form tetramers
items.why: With only one functioning alpha gene, the unpaired beta chains in adults combine into tetramers. **Hb H is a beta4 tetramer formed when three of the four alpha genes are lost.** Hb H is unstable and precipitates as many small inclusions with brilliant cresyl blue, giving a golf-ball appearance.

whyNot.0: Loss of two alpha genes causes alpha-thalassemia trait, usually with mild microcytosis and no Hb H.
whyNot.1: Loss of all four alpha genes causes Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis, in which the fetus forms gamma4 tetramers.
whyNot.3: Gamma4 tetramers are Hb Bart's; they may be seen at birth, but Hb H itself is made of beta chains.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on thalassemias

items.stem: A 72-year-old has a lymphocyte count of 45 x 10^9/L made up of small, mature-looking lymphocytes and many smudge cells. Flow cytometry shows CD19+, CD5+, and CD23+ cells with weak surface immunoglobulin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: CLL is a neoplasm of small mature B cells, and smudge cells are common on the smear because the cells are fragile. **Co-expression of CD5 and CD23 on B cells with weak surface immunoglobulin is the characteristic CLL phenotype.**

whyNot.0: Mantle cell lymphoma is also CD5-positive, but it is usually CD23-negative and expresses cyclin D1.
whyNot.1: Hairy cell leukemia shows CD11c, CD25, and CD103 and usually presents with pancytopenia, not marked lymphocytosis.
whyNot.2: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma cells are usually negative for both CD5 and CD23 and often have short villous projections.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on mature lymphoid neoplasms

items.stem: An adult has fever, confusion, a platelet count of 15 x 10^9/L, many schistocytes, and a high LDH. The PT, APTT, and fibrinogen are normal. Which defect most likely underlies this disorder?
options: Severely reduced ADAMTS13 activity, leaving ultralarge VWF multimers
Consumption of clotting factors after widespread tissue factor release
Antibodies against platelet factor 4-heparin complexes on platelets
Shiga toxin injury to the glomerular endothelium of the kidney
items.why: The findings point to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: microangiopathic hemolysis and severe thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation tests. **Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultralarge VWF multimers uncleaved, so platelets aggregate in small vessels.** Normal PT, APTT, and fibrinogen distinguish it from DIC.

whyNot.1: Tissue factor-driven factor consumption describes DIC, which prolongs the PT and APTT and lowers fibrinogen.
whyNot.2: PF4-heparin antibodies cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs heparin exposure and does not usually produce schistocytes.
whyNot.3: Shiga toxin causes typical hemolytic uremic syndrome, mainly in children after bloody diarrhea, with prominent renal failure and normal ADAMTS13.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on thrombocytopenia and thrombotic microangiopathies

items.stem: Which coagulation factor is a transglutaminase that cross-links fibrin to stabilize the clot?
items.why: Thrombin activates factor XIII, which in the presence of calcium forms covalent bonds between neighboring fibrin molecules. **Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin**, making the clot strong and resistant to fibrinolysis.

whyNot.1: Factor XI is an intrinsic pathway serine protease that activates factor IX.
whyNot.2: Factor XII is a contact factor that starts the intrinsic pathway in vitro.
whyNot.3: Factor X, once activated, joins factor Va to convert prothrombin to thrombin.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on normal hemostasis and coagulation

items.stem: Heparin's anticoagulant effect depends on a natural plasma inhibitor. Which inhibitor does heparin accelerate, and which factors does that inhibitor mainly neutralize?
options: Protein C, which inactivates factors Va and VIIIa
Antithrombin, which neutralizes thrombin and factor Xa
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor, which blocks factor VIIa
items.why: Antithrombin is a serine protease inhibitor that slowly inactivates thrombin, factor Xa, and other activated serine proteases. **Heparin binds antithrombin and speeds its action more than 1000-fold**, so a patient with antithrombin deficiency may respond poorly to heparin.

whyNot.0: Protein C inactivates factors Va and VIIIa, but it is activated by thrombin-thrombomodulin, not by heparin.
whyNot.2: Alpha-2-antiplasmin controls fibrinolysis by neutralizing plasmin; it is not a heparin cofactor.
whyNot.3: TFPI inhibits the tissue factor-VIIa-Xa complex and is not the main target of heparin therapy.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on normal hemostasis and coagulation (coagulation regulatory mechanisms)

items.stem: During cardiopulmonary bypass, a patient receives very high doses of unfractionated heparin. Which point-of-care test is used in the operating room to monitor this heparin?
items.why: The activated clotting time is a whole-blood clotting test performed beside the patient with a contact activator. **The ACT stays measurable at the very high heparin levels used in bypass surgery and gives results within minutes.**

whyNot.0: At bypass heparin levels the APTT becomes unclottable, so it cannot guide dosing.
whyNot.1: The PT is relatively insensitive to heparin and is used to monitor warfarin.
whyNot.3: The anti-Xa assay is a laboratory test that takes too long for minute-to-minute decisions in the operating room.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on antithrombotic therapy and laboratory monitoring

items.stem: In a one-stage factor VIII assay (APTT with factor VIII-deficient plasma), a patient's factor VIII activity, corrected for dilution, is 8% at 1:10, 15% at 1:20, and 27% at 1:40. What does this pattern suggest?
options: An inhibitor in the patient plasma whose effect lessens as it is diluted
Factor VIII activity of about 17%, the average of the three dilutions
Tissue factor contamination from a traumatic draw activating the specimen
Factor VIII activity of about 27%, since the most dilute result is the most accurate
items.why: Results from different dilutions should agree (be parallel) once corrected for dilution. **Activity that rises with each further dilution indicates an inhibitor, such as a lupus anticoagulant or a factor VIII antibody, that is being diluted out.** The result should not be reported as a single value; inhibitor studies are needed.

whyNot.1: Averaging nonparallel results hides the inhibitor and gives a number that reflects no true activity.
whyNot.2: Activation shortens clotting times and gives higher activity at the least dilute level, which is the opposite pattern.
whyNot.3: Choosing the highest value ignores the nonparallel pattern, which itself shows that an inhibitor is present.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on laboratory evaluation of hemostasis (factor assays); CLSI H48 (Determination of Coagulation Factor Activities Using the One-Stage Clotting Assay)

items.stem: A patient has a prolonged PT and a normal APTT, and the PT corrects on a 1:1 mix with normal plasma. A deficiency of which single factor best explains these results?
items.why: The PT measures factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen, while the APTT measures the intrinsic and common pathway factors. **Factor VII is the only factor measured by the PT and not by the APTT**, so its deficiency prolongs the PT alone; correction on mixing confirms a deficiency rather than an inhibitor.

whyNot.1: Factor VIII deficiency prolongs the APTT and leaves the PT normal.
whyNot.2: Factor X is in the common pathway, so its deficiency prolongs both the PT and the APTT.
whyNot.3: Factor XII deficiency prolongs only the APTT.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on laboratory evaluation of hemostasis

items.stem: A patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics with no oral intake for a week develops vitamin K deficiency. The PT is prolonged while the APTT is still normal. Why does the PT become abnormal first?
options: Factor VII is the only vitamin K-dependent factor that the PT measures
Factor VII has the shortest half-life of the vitamin K-dependent factors
APTT reagents do not respond to deficiencies of factors II, IX, and X
Protein C falls first, and the PT is sensitive to protein C deficiency
items.why: Vitamin K is needed for gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X. **Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 4 to 6 hours)**, so its level drops first and the PT, which is sensitive to factor VII, prolongs before the APTT. The same is seen early in warfarin therapy.

whyNot.0: The PT also measures the vitamin K-dependent factors II and X, not only factor VII.
whyNot.2: The APTT does respond to factors II, IX, and X; it changes later because those factors decline more slowly.
whyNot.3: Protein C is an anticoagulant and is not measured by the PT, so its fall does not prolong clotting time.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on disorders of secondary hemostasis (acquired coagulation disorders)

items.stem: The factor V Leiden mutation is a common inherited cause of venous thrombosis. How does it increase thrombotic risk?
options: Factor Va resists inhibition by antithrombin
Factor Va resists cleavage by activated protein C
Prothrombin is overproduced because of a gene variant
Protein S is produced in a nonfunctional form
items.why: Factor V Leiden is a single amino acid change (Arg506Gln) at a cleavage site for activated protein C. **The mutant factor Va resists inactivation by activated protein C**, so it keeps generating thrombin longer. The laboratory screens with an APC resistance assay and confirms with DNA testing.

whyNot.0: Antithrombin mainly neutralizes thrombin and factor Xa; factor Va is regulated by protein C.
whyNot.2: Increased prothrombin from a gene variant describes the prothrombin G20210A mutation, a different thrombophilia.
whyNot.3: Protein S deficiency is a separate inherited thrombophilia that reduces the cofactor activity for protein C.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on thrombophilia

items.stem: A single hemoglobin control value falls at +3.4 SD from the mean. Earlier values were all within plus or minus 1 SD. Under Westgard multirule criteria, how should this be handled?
options: A 1-2s warning only; accept the run and keep monitoring
A 2-2s violation suggesting systematic error; reject the run
A 1-3s violation suggesting random error; reject the run
A 10x violation suggesting a shift; recalibrate the analyzer
items.why: The 1-3s rule is violated when one control value exceeds 3 SD from the mean. **A 1-3s violation is a rejection rule that mainly signals random error**, so patient results from the run are held while the cause is found and corrected.

whyNot.0: Although the value also exceeds 2 SD, any value beyond 3 SD is a rejection signal, not just a warning.
whyNot.1: The 2-2s rule needs two consecutive values beyond 2 SD on the same side; only one value is out here.
whyNot.3: The 10x rule needs ten consecutive values on one side of the mean, which has not happened.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 7th ed., chapter on quality assurance in hematology and hemostasis testing; Westgard multirule QC
